explain.say: USB-C has a special configuration wire. Over it, the charger can list what it is able to supply, such as 9, 15 or 20 volts, and the phone or laptop chooses what it needs. This conversation is called USB Power Delivery.

faq.q: Why does USB start at 5 volts?
faq.a: Five volts is the original USB standard, safe for every USB device ever made. A charger only raises the voltage after the device has asked for more, so an old gadget can never be given too much.

faq.q: What does the CC wire in USB-C do?
faq.a: The configuration channel wire tells each end that a cable is plugged in, which way round it is, and carries the Power Delivery messages where the charger and device agree on power.
asks: How does USB-C know which way round it is?

faq.a: USB Power Delivery is the set of rules for that conversation. The charger lists its options, the device requests one, the charger accepts, and only then switches to the new voltage. It allows up to 240 watts.
asks: How does USB-C fast charging work?

faq.q: Why do some USB cables charge slower?
faq.a: Cables have thin wires that heat up if too much current flows. Most are rated for 3 amps; only cables with an electronic marker chip are trusted to carry 5 amps, so the charger limits power to suit the cable.
asks: Do USB cables matter for charging speed?

faq.q: Can a big laptop charger damage my phone?
faq.a: No. The charger only provides the voltage the phone asks for, and the phone's own charging chip controls how much current goes into its battery. A bigger charger just has more available.
asks: Is it safe to charge my phone with a laptop charger?

facts: USB Power Delivery 3.1 allows up to 240 watts, using 48 volts at 5 amps.
USB-C cables rated for 5 amps carry an electronic marker (e-marker) chip.
